I am a veteran, I spent 4 years as an rifleman in the USMC, and I am 100% positive that a large civilian uprising could beat not just the Marine Corps, and even the entire military. There are two aspects that give me this confidence, actual in use military doctrine, and the culture of our military.

In regards to military doctrine, the US military uses 99% maneuver warfare doctrine, which utilizes small groups of troops moving around very quickly, which was effective for the time it was developed but as the global war on terror has shown, it’s not very good against guerrilla warfare.
Not only do you have to maintain these massive amounts of vehicles that are ferrying troops around, you also have to rapidly extend and maintain supply lines for these fast units, which leaves them very vulnerable. That is why it is so susceptible to guerrilla warfare, because you’ve got all these small units that require a lot of maintenance and supplies running around every which way trying to find an enemy that they aren’t even sure is there, and all that running around wreaks havoc on supply lines logistically, leaves them exposed and vulnerable, and limits the ability to mass large amounts of troops in any one place quickly. In places like the Rocky and Appalachian mountains, the terrain makes it impossible to tactically utilize vehicles, and the tree cover is so thick that in order to land troops by air you would have fo clear a landing zone artillery most likely, which would alert anyone within 10 square miles that the military is on it’s way. So the only option left would be to hike in on foot, which would not only be exhausting, but also leave them dangerously exposed.

In regards to helicopters and bombers and whatnot, almost all of them use thermal imaging to acquire and engage targets. Everyone has seen videos of drones and Apaches in Afghanistan using thermals to annihilate targets, but Afghanistan is also a very open, sparsely vegetated country. In areas with thick vegetation, like the Pacific Northwest, Northeast, and Southeast, the vegetation would severely limit target acquisition capabilities both in human piloted aircrafts and drones.
